newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani rupee seen pressed by inflation.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani rupee seen pressed by inflation.

text.p: The Pakistani rupee is likely to weaken further before the end of fiscal 1996/97 (July-June) after the State (central) Bank of Pakistan slashed its value by 0.29 percent on Wednesday, analysts said.
The central bank adjusted the rupee down to 40.2400/40.4412 to the dollar from the 40.1200/40.3206 fixed on October 22 when it depreciated the rupee by 7.86 percent.

The central bank gave no reason for the lower adjustment, but bankers said the move was expected as the dollar had appreciated quite sharply against other currencies while Pakistan's inflation figures had shown a rising trend.
The rupee, after Wednesday's adjustment, had depreciated by 14.43 percent since the beginning of fiscal 1996/97 compared to a depreciation of 13.2 percent in the year-ago period.
"Our assessment is that the rupee will depreciate by another 2.7 percent by end June," Anisur Rehman, research head of SocGen Crosby Securities, told Reuters.
He said the main reason for the pressure on the rupee value was rising inflation over the past six months.
Food prices have jumped in recent weeks amid an unprecedented wheat flour shortage that sparked violence in many cities, he said.
The consumer price index (CPI) rose 11.8 percent in March from 10.27 percent in March 1996 while the wholesale price index (WPI) jumped 13.4 percent.
"With the recent increase in food prices CPI could easily rise up to 12.5 percent for April which leaves the rupee extremely uncompetitive," Rehman said.

The chief economist of a foreign bank, who asked not to be named, said the adjustment was expected as the nominal and real effective exchange rates for the rupee had appreciated quite significantly since the last devaluation.
"This was expected because since October Pakistan has witnessed a high rate of inflation while the U.S. dollar has been strong in the international market," he said.
The economist said the government, if it wanted to appease international donors and Pakistani exporters, was likely to follow a pro-active exchange rate system instead of large devaluations.
"It seems the government had initiated a crawling peg devaluation policy so that the rupee does not appreciate in real terms while there is no panic in the kerb market," he said.
The rupee opened 0.10 lower at 41.10 to the dollar in the kerb market on news of the adjustment.
Dealer Ovais Kalia said the central bank was likely to devalue the rupee by another three to four percent until the announcement of the 1997/98 (July-June) budget in June.
Analyst Zuna Mansoor of ING Baring Securities said the lower adjustment of the rupee was small and might not have an impact on the stock market.
But she said the cautious foreign portfolio investor might continue a wait-and-see approach as more adjustments were expected.
